cmimc-2026-algebra-01.title: Divisibility on the leftover
cmimc-2026-algebra-01.body:
Let $N$ be the starting number of candies. The leftover is $N-\frac N4-\frac N6-\frac N8=\frac{11N}{24}$.

It must be a whole number divisible by $4$ (split among four people). So $N$ is a multiple of $24$; write $N=24k$. The leftover is $11k$, and $4\mid 11k$ forces $4\mid k$. The smallest choice is $k=4$, giving $N=96$ (leftover $44$, each of the four gets $11$).

**Answer: $96$**

cmimc-2026-algebra-01.title: Check the candidates directly
cmimc-2026-algebra-01.body:
$N$ must be divisible by $4$, $6$ and $8$, so by $24$: $N=24,48,72,96,\dots$ with leftovers $11,22,33,44,\dots$ (that is, $11N/24$). The first leftover divisible by $4$ is $44$, at $N=96$.

**Answer: $96$**

cmimc-2026-algebra-02.title: Make the other days as cold as possible
cmimc-2026-algebra-02.body:
The $12$ temperatures sum to $12\cdot 23=276$. To make the hottest day as large as possible, make the other $11$ temperatures as small as possible. Each value may be used at most twice and the minimum is $15$, so the smallest choice is
$$15,15,16,16,17,17,18,18,19,19,20,$$
with sum $2(15+16+17+18+19)+20=170+20=190$.

The hottest day is then at most $276-190=86$, and $86$ is achieved by this list together with $86$ (it appears once and the minimum is still $15$).

**Answer: $86$**

cmimc-2026-algebra-03.title: Cubes sum to the square of the integer sum
cmimc-2026-algebra-03.body:
Let $N=2^{89}-1$. Then $k=\frac{N(N+1)}2=(2^{89}-1)\cdot 2^{88}$.

The number of divisors of $2^{88}\cdot N$ is $89\cdot d(N)$ if $N$ is odd (it is) and coprime to $2$, so $89\,d(N)=178$ gives $d(N)=2$: $N=2^{89}-1$ is prime.

Since $1^3+\dots+N^3=\left(\frac{N(N+1)}2\right)^2=k^2$, we get $n=2^{176}\cdot N^2$ with $N$ an odd prime. Hence
$$d(n)=(176+1)(2+1)=531.$$

**Answer: $531$**

cmimc-2026-algebra-05.title: Difference of squares
cmimc-2026-algebra-05.body:
Write $\sqrt{1024+3p}=32+k$ with $k>0$ an integer. Then $1024+64k+k^2=1024+3p$, so
$$k(k+64)=3p.$$
Since $p$ is prime, $k$ divides $3p$, so $k\in\{1,3,p,3p\}$. For $k=p$ or $3p$ the factor $k+64$ would have to be $3$ or $1$, impossible. For $k=1$: $65=3p$, impossible. For $k=3$: $3\cdot67=3p$, so $p=67$ (indeed $1024+201=1225=35^2$).

So the only prime is $67$.

**Answer: $67$**

cmimc-2026-algebra-06.title: Lucas' theorem
cmimc-2026-algebra-06.body:
Count the entries **not** divisible by $3$ and subtract from $2027$.

Write $2026$ in base $3$: $2026=2\cdot729+2\cdot243+1\cdot81+0+0+0+1$, i.e. $(2210001)_3$.

By Lucas' theorem, $\binom{2026}{j}\not\equiv0\pmod 3$ exactly when each base-$3$ digit of $j$ is at most the corresponding digit of $2026$. The number of such $j$ is $\prod(d_i+1)=3\cdot3\cdot2\cdot1\cdot1\cdot1\cdot2=36$.

Hence the number of multiples of $3$ is $2027-36=1991$ (also confirmed by direct computation).

**Answer: $1991$**

cmimc-2026-algebra-07.title: Factor the conic
cmimc-2026-algebra-07.body:
Since $3x^2+4xy+y^2+2x+4y-5=(3x+y+5)(x+y-1)$, the congruence is $(3x+y+5)(x+y-1)\equiv-4\pmod{83}$.

Let $z=x+y-1$; then $3x+y+5=z+2x+6$, so $z(z+2x+6)\equiv-4$. Thus $z\not\equiv0$ and
$$2x\equiv-\left(z+6+\frac4z\right),\qquad x\equiv-\left(\frac z2+3+\frac2z\right)\pmod{83}.$$
Conversely, every nonzero $z$ gives a solution (take that $x$ and $y=z+1-x$).

So we count the distinct values of $f(z)=\frac z2+\frac2z$ over nonzero $z$. We have $f(z)=f(z')$ iff $(z-z')\left(\frac12-\frac2{zz'}\right)=0$, i.e. $z'=z$ or $z'=\frac4z$. The involution $z\mapsto4/z$ has exactly two fixed points $z=\pm2$, and the other $80$ nonzero residues pair up into $40$ pairs. Hence there are $2+40=42$ distinct $x$.

**Answer: $42$**

cmimc-2026-algebra-07.title: Direct computation
cmimc-2026-algebra-07.body:
Running through all pairs $(x,y)$ with $0\le x,y<83$ and testing the congruence gives exactly $42$ values of $x$ having at least one solution $y$.

**Answer: $42$**

cmimc-2026-algebra-08.title: Roots of a polynomial from $\tan 9\alpha=0$
cmimc-2026-algebra-08.body:
If $\tan9\alpha=0$ then $\operatorname{Im}(1+ix)^9=0$ with $x=\tan\alpha$, i.e.
$$9x-84x^3+126x^5-36x^7+x^9=0.$$
The solutions are $x=\tan\alpha$ for $\alpha=0^\circ,20^\circ,\dots,160^\circ$. Dividing by $x$ and putting $t=x^2$ gives
$$t^4-36t^3+126t^2-84t+9=0,$$
whose roots are $t_i=\tan^2\alpha$ for $\alpha=20^\circ,40^\circ,60^\circ,80^\circ$.

Then $\sum t_i=36$ and $\sum_{i<j}t_it_j=126$, so
$$\sum t_i^2=36^2-2\cdot126=1296-252=1044.$$

**Answer: $1044$**

cmimc-2026-algebra-09.title: Count by divisors
cmimc-2026-algebra-09.body:
$\sum_{n\le N}f(n)=\sum_{d\le N}d\left\lfloor \frac Nd\right\rfloor=\sum_{m\le N}\frac{\lfloor N/m\rfloor(\lfloor N/m\rfloor+1)}2$.

Heuristically this is about $\frac{\pi^2}{12}N^2\approx 8.22\times10^7$. Evaluating the exact sum for $N=10000$ by computer gives $82256014$. The official key states the same value; closer estimates score better.

**Answer: $82256014$**
